name: Spring Onion
lede: Spring Onion is a fresh, moderate yellow-green, the color of the tender shoots, listed in our library from a Japanese traditional color set.

sections.title: A shoot's green
sections.body:
The name belongs to a plant, and the swatch is the spring-shoot green between a leaf green and a pale lime [1]. Our library takes it from a Japanese traditional color set, with no date and no further note on its origin [1]. The ISCC-NBS system files the swatch under "moderate yellow green", 7.7 CIEDE2000 units away, a loose fit [1].

The only mention in our books concerns the smell, not the color. Finlay describes placing a live purple-dye snail, a caracola, on his watch strap, where it soon turned bright purple and gave off a strong smell of spring onions [2]. That tells us about the dye animal, and nothing about this green [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Spring Onion is rare in painting [3]. It appears in 17 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, 0.07 per cent, rarer than 65 per cent of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 0.3 per cent of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 3.6 times the museums' baseline [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 54 per cent of the 13 paintings where the within-painting lens finds it [3].

The earliest dated match is 1861 and the latest 1913, and the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue and not proof of a pigment [3]. In printed English the words peak in the 2010s [4].
